edition: Issue 022 - A $6 million billing oops, a Mars rock nobody can afford to fetch, and Auckland arguing about the trains again
tagline: Your 3-minute break. Zero fluff, maximum banter.

stories.headline: Watercare deeply sorry after taking $6.14m out of 44,000 accounts, 18 days early
stories.summary: A billing-system upgrade glitch saw Watercare charge 43,835 Auckland customers a combined $6.14 million up to 18 days before their bills were due, with refunds offered only on request.

body.text: Watercare mistakenly billed 43,835 Auckland customers 18 days early, deducting a combined $6.14 million from their accounts on Monday. The company said an error during an upgrade to its billing system processed direct debits and credit-card payments before their due dates. Chief financial officer Angela Neeson apologised, said affected customers were contacted the same day, and offered to reverse payments for anyone facing hardship, but customers who took the refund would then need to manually pay their bill on the original due date.

There is a special kind of we-are-sorry that only a monopoly can produce. Watercare, the company that owns your pipes, pulled $6 million out of 44,000 people accounts eighteen days early, and its solution is: if you really cant cope, ask us nicely and well hand it back, as long as you promise to pay us again later, by hand, all by yourself. Thats not a refund, thats a round-trip ticket to the guilt trip. Credit where its due, though: describing a $6m glitch as an upgrade is the most New Zealand corporate spin since the road was wet.

RNZ / Stuff / NZ Herald (13-14 Oct 2026): Watercare CFO Angela Neeson confirmed 43,835 customer accounts were charged approximately $6.14 million prematurely during a billing-system upgrade, with payments processed up to 18 days before their due date. Customers facing hardship were offered reversals, returned the same day or next working day, but would then pay the amount manually on the due date. Consumer NZs Jessica Walker called it a likely failure of reasonable care and skill under the Consumer Guarantees Act.

stories.headline: The most exciting rock in the universe is sealed in a tube on Mars, and nobody can afford to go get it
stories.summary: NASAs Perseverance rover sealed a sample its own science team calls a potential biosignature, but the mission meant to bring it home was cancelled over cost, leaving an unprecedented Mars sample stuck in storage.

body.text: NASAs Perseverance rover is holding a sealed rock sample, called Sapphire Canyon, drilled from a Mars rock its science team describes as a potential biosignature, the strongest lead yet toward evidence of past life on another planet. But the Mars Sample Return program meant to bring it to Earth was cancelled after its cost estimates ballooned to as much as $11 billion, so the sample could sit in its tube indefinitely. Chinas Tianwen-3 mission, meanwhile, is targeting its own Mars sample return by 2031.

This is the most exciting rock in the history of the universe, and the mission to fetch it was cancelled because it got too expensive and complicated, which is a deeply human tragedy relocated to Mars: we figured out the big thing, and no one wants to pay the courier. Scientists are now watching Chinas rival mission with the energy of someone who did all the homework and watched the other group do the presentation. It all boils down to one line: the rocks are there, theyre in their tubes, all we have got to do is go get them.

RNZ / CNN (13 Oct 2026): Perseverance collected the Sapphire Canyon sample from a rock called Cheyava Falls in Jezero Crater; science-team member Adrian Broz called it the first thing the rover found that qualifies as a potential biosignature. NASA cancelled the Mars Sample Return program in its FY26 budget request after spending roughly $2.5 billion, with overall cost estimates reaching up to $11 billion. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has said he wants the samples returned; Chinas Tianwen-3 mission targets a Mars sample return by 2031.

stories.headline: All Blacks beat Australia, then Auckland spends a week arguing about who owns the blame for the trains
stories.summary: Rail delays left about 15,000 fans waiting up to 40 minutes to leave the Bledisloe Cup at Eden Park; the stadium boss wants a footbridge, the mayor says it is Eden Parks own fault.

body.text: After the All Blacks Bledisloe Cup win over Australia at Eden Park on Saturday, rail delays left hundreds of fans waiting up to 40 minutes to get home, with Auckland Transport saying about 15,000 people used rail for the game. Eden Park boss Nick Sautner called for platform upgrades and a pedestrian footbridge. Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown hit back, calling the footbridge push inappropriate and disappointing, blaming the late closure of a level crossing by Eden Parks own traffic contractors, and saying ratepayers should not fund a costly project prompted by a single incident.

Everyones favourite Auckland ritual: 48,000 of you beat Australia, and then the two loudest men in the city spend the week arguing about whose to blame for the trains while the rest of you wait 40 minutes on the platform at Kingsland. The mayor says its an operational screw-up, the stadium boss wants a bridge, and both of them are absolutely certain that someone else should pay for it. At least the All Blacks gave everyone something to fight about on the way home.

RNZ (13 Oct 2026): Auckland Transport said about 15,000 people used rail to and from the All Blacks vs Wallabies Bledisloe Cup test at Eden Park on Saturday 10 October; delays left hundreds of fans waiting up to 40 minutes, primarily at Kingsland Station. Eden Park boss Nick Sautner backed platform upgrades and a footbridge; Mayor Wayne Brown said an initial audit indicated the Morningside Drive level crossing was closed later than the approved Traffic Management Plan allowed, by Eden Parks own contractor, calling it an operational rather than infrastructure issue.

affiliate_cta.headline: Planning a move or a big one-off bill? Here is what we would look at.
affiliate_cta.body: Between a monopoly taking money out of your account two weeks early, a space program that could not afford the courier, and a rail network apparently allergic to match days, this edition is a reminder that the small, boring safeguards hold up best. No pitch, no pressure: just a calm look before you commit to anything.
